planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil; this hybrid tolerates drier, leaner sites than most bee balms and resents heavy, waterlogged clay.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this cross between wild bergamot and the Mexican species Monarda bartlettii arose in a Texas garden and combines the hardiness of fistulosa with a much stronger resistance to powdery mildew than most garden bee balms. Whorled lavender-purple flowers with dark purple calyces top the clumps from midsummer into fall and draw hummingbirds and a steady stream of bumblebees. It performs best where humidity is high but soil drains freely, and unlike Monarda didyma selections it shrugs off heat and dry spells once established. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor and airflow through the foliage.

planting.note: Set out container plants after last frost in gritty, well-drained soil; good winter drainage matters far more to survival than added fertility.

directions: Plant in lean to average, sharply drained soil in full sun; this selection from Limerock Plant Farm carries deep ruby-red, gold-centered daisies over fine, threadlike foliage from early summer well into fall. It is among the darkest-flowered tickseeds available and spreads gently by rhizome without becoming weedy, making it useful for edging or containers. Shear lightly after the first flush to encourage rebloom, and site it where winter wet will not sit around the crown, since rot rather than cold is the main threat to its survival in colder zones. Established plants are drought tolerant and largely ignored by deer and rabbits.

planting.note: Scarify and sow where plants are to remain, or set out young transplants while the taproot is still small; established plants resent being moved.

directions: Plant in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this larger-leaved prairie and open-woodland variety of white wild indigo forms a broad, shrub-like clump of blue-green trifoliate foliage topped by tall white candelabra spikes in early summer. Once the deep taproot is established it needs no supplemental watering or staking and can be left undisturbed for decades, slowly building presence rather than spreading aggressively. The blackened seed pods that follow bloom persist into winter and add architectural interest, and the flowers are an important early-season resource for bumblebees. Give it room at planting time, since a mature clump is heavier and wider than the species type.

planting.note: Sow in fall to satisfy the cold stratification the corms need, or plant nursery-propagated stock in a sharply drained, gritty site that mimics its native rock outcrops.

directions: Plant in lean, gravelly or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; this diminutive blazing star is native only to a handful of high-elevation rock outcrops in the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, where it grows from a small corm wedged into thin, acidic soil pockets. It produces a short, dense spike of rose-purple flowers in late summer that is proportionally larger than the compact foliage below it, and it depends on excellent drainage year-round to avoid crown rot. Because it is federally listed as threatened in the wild, plants offered in the trade should be nursery-propagated from cultivated stock rather than wild-collected. It is best suited to a rock garden or scree bed rather than a typical perennial border.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock from a reputable native plant source in spring or fall in shallow, clay-based or rocky soil; avoid disturbing any wild populations, as this species is federally endangered.

directions: Plant in shallow, clay-rich or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Short's goldenrod is a globally rare species now restricted to a small area of Kentucky around Blue Licks, where it grows on thin-soiled limestone slopes and cedar glade openings. In cultivation it behaves as a well-mannered, clump-forming goldenrod, producing bright yellow flower clusters from late summer into fall that are heavily visited by native bees and migrating butterflies. It tolerates the periodic disturbance and thin soils that would stress lusher garden perennials, but appreciates full sun and freedom from tall competing vegetation. Only plant material propagated from cultivated stock should be used, in keeping with its endangered status in the wild.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this high-elevation species prefers cooler summer conditions than the lowland Joe Pye weeds.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial sun to light shade; Appalachian Joe Pye weed is native to cool seeps and moist woodland openings at higher elevations in the southern Appalachians, where it forms tall, purple-green stems topped by broad, dome-shaped clusters of mauve-pink flowers in late summer. It is closely related to E. purpureum but tends to hold its color and stem strength better in the humid, part-shaded conditions typical of mountain coves, and it draws swallowtails and other large butterflies in numbers. Give it steady soil moisture through summer and avoid hot, exposed sites, since it is adapted to cooler microclimates than the more widespread lowland Joe Pye weeds. Established clumps need no staking and can be divided every few years to control size.

planting.note: Sow into sharply drained, gravelly soil or set out young transplants in spring; a calcareous, low-fertility site closest to its native piñon-juniper habitat gives the best long-term performance.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun; cardinal penstemon is native to canyon bottoms and rocky slopes of the Sacramento and Capitan mountains of New Mexico, where it sends up spreading, woody-based stems tipped with tall spikes of deep blood-red, tubular flowers over a long midsummer bloom period. The intense red color and tubular shape make it one of the most reliable hummingbird plants among the beardtongues, and it is markedly more heat- and alkalinity-tolerant than eastern Penstemon species. It is a moderately short-lived perennial that often self-sows lightly in gravelly, open ground, so allow a few volunteer seedlings to develop to maintain a planting over time. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils, which shorten its lifespan and encourage floppy growth.
